posts.title: The Morning Cut: Butchering for the Evening Coals
posts.excerpt: Head butcher Mara Lindqvist and second butcher Priya Nair break down whole loins each morning at nine so that nothing served across our evening charcoal grills is older than the day.
posts.content:
At nine in the morning, the Harlow Quarter is quiet. Deliveries rattle down Ostrand Street, and inside Sumibi Yakiniku, the lights over the stainless steel butchery counter are already switched on. Mara Lindqvist, our founder and head butcher, ties her apron while Priya Nair unwraps the day’s arrival of whole beef loins. There is no music and very little conversation. The work requires cool hands, sharp carbon steel, and complete focus on the grain of the meat. Every cut that will touch our table grills tonight begins on this timber-backed cutting block.

Our butchery philosophy has remained unchanged since we opened our doors in 2012. We do not purchase pre-portioned steaks, frozen vacuum-sealed strips, or cuts trimmed elsewhere. Mara and Priya break down whole primal cuts from the bone, reading the fat distribution and muscle seam of each individual loin. Different sections demand different treatments: some portions are trimmed lean for high-heat searing, while heavily marbled sections are reserved for our longer courses. Because every carcass yields distinct textures, the butchers adjust their slicing angles by fractions of a millimeter to ensure tenderness across the fire.

By midday, the primary breakdown is complete, and Priya begins the precise work of portioning and plating. Each cut is destined for one of our four evening offerings: the 9-plate Evening Course at €48, the 11-plate Butcher’s Course at €68, the 13-plate Whole Coal Course at €92, or the 10-plate Group Table Course at €58. Thin ribbons of salted tongue, rich outside skirt, and dense short rib are arranged cleanly across cold earthenware plates. Three morning cuts from today’s loins are set aside specifically for the Butcher’s Course, showcasing the fresh, clean profile that only same-day butchering can provide.

Everything is sliced, portioned, and plated by 16:00. This strict timeline ensures that the meat rests at cellar temperature before dinner service begins, allowing the marbling to soften gently without losing moisture. Our rule is absolute: nothing served on the evening plates is older than the day. We never freeze unsold portions, and what is not cut this morning will never appear on tonight’s menu. If a particular cut is exhausted during service, that cut is done for the night. This discipline ensures that every guest tastes beef at its peak vitality.

At 17:00, the atmosphere shifts from cold butchery to heat. Grill master Tomás Reyes and charcoal specialist Sam Whitlock enter the floor to light the coals for all 18 table grills and the 10-seat counter. In forty minutes, before our doors open at 17:30, thirty kilograms of oak charcoal turn into glowing embers. When our senior server Rafael Duarte lays the first thin slice of morning-cut loin over the grate, the intense dry radiant heat immediately sears the surface. The rendered fat drips into the coals and returns upward as savory smoke, completing the quiet circle that began at nine o’clock.

posts.title: Coals at five
posts.excerpt: Tomás and Sam light 18 grills and the counter in forty minutes, every day before the doors open.
posts.content:
At five o’clock every afternoon the dining room is empty and quiet, and the work that gives the evening its character begins. Tomás Reyes, our grill master, and Sam Whitlock, who looks after the charcoal and the ventilation, carry the first baskets of lit coals in from the yard. The charcoal arrives in paper sacks, dense hardwood that burns hot and clean, and it is lit in steel chimney starters behind the building, well before it goes near a table.

Each of the eighteen table grills and the ten seats at the counter gets its own basket. Tomás lowers it into the grill well, spreads the coals with a long steel rake, and listens. He says the sound tells him more than the colour does: a dry, even crackle means the coals are ready, while a hiss means they are still giving off moisture. Sam follows behind with a hand held over each well to check the heat, then opens or closes the dampers on the hood above it so the smoke is drawn upward rather than across the table.

The whole room takes about forty minutes. By a quarter past five the grills are glowing, the hoods are humming, and the room smells of warm charcoal rather than of cooking. That is the signal the floor team waits for. Rafael Duarte and the other servers set the tables, light the lamps, and walk through the room once, looking at every grill from a guest’s side of the table. If a basket has settled unevenly, Tomás is called back to fix it. Doors open at half past five, and from that moment the coals belong to the guests.

Why light them so early? Because charcoal that is lit at the moment a guest sits down is still unsteady, flaring and then collapsing, and a grill in that state is hard to cook on. A coal bed that has had forty minutes to settle gives an even, dry heat that stays level for the best part of two hours, long enough for a full course without anyone needing to tend the fire. It also means that the first slice of the evening goes onto a grate that is already exactly as hot as the last slice will need. This is the same every day we are open, six evenings a week, and it is why our reservations line closes at five: by then the whole house is busy lighting the room.

posts.title: The long table
posts.excerpt: A 24-guest retirement dinner on the Upper Floor, booked by Amara three weeks ahead.
posts.content:
In March a retirement dinner for twenty-four guests took over the Upper Floor. It was booked three weeks in advance by Amara Osei, our floor manager, who handles every group and private-room booking herself. The host, a teacher leaving a school after thirty years, had written to the reservations address with a date, a headcount, and a single request: that everyone should be able to talk to everyone.

That is the question we ask first with any large booking. The Upper Floor can be set with two rows of grills, one on each side of a long table, so that the room works as one table rather than several. Amara walked the host through the plan, chose the Group Table Course at €58 per guest, ten shared plates over two hours, and held the floor for forty-eight hours while the host confirmed numbers with her colleagues. Groups of eight or more book at least seven days ahead and choose one course for the whole table; it keeps the kitchen steady and the grills moving at one pace.

On the evening itself the coals were lit at five as always, but Tomás set the Upper Floor grills slightly lower than usual, because a long table of talkers cooks more slowly than a table of two. Rafael Duarte led the service and brought each plate to the middle of the table rather than to individual places, so that guests passed them along by hand. The beef arrived in three waves, thin cuts first, then the thicker cuts Mara had sliced that morning, then the ribeye. Lena Fischer built a four-glass pairing for the course, served at the table in the same order.

Afterwards the host wrote to say that what she remembered was not any one dish but the noise: twenty-four people leaning over the same grates, reaching across each other with tongs. We take that as the best description of what a group booking here is for. If you are planning something similar, the Hearth Room seats eight around a round table with two grills, the Long Room seats twelve at one long timber table, and the Upper Floor takes up to twenty-four, with its own entrance. Write to us with a date and a headcount, and Amara will reply the same day.
